title: Indexes
subtitle: How the database jumps instead of scanning — and what it charges you
objectives: Explain what an index is and why it turns a scan into ~20 steps
Describe why databases use B-trees, and what sortedness buys you
Account for the real cost of an index: writes, disk, and when the planner ignores it
Design a composite index for a real query — right columns, right order — and verify with `EXPLAIN`

exercises.title: An index is a second, sorted copy of one column that says where the row is
exercises.body: The index at the back of a book is separate from the text, sorted, and much smaller — so you find "sharding" by flipping to S rather than reading 1,000 pages. A database index is that same object: a sorted structure mapping one column's values to row locations. Sorted means you can bisect, and bisecting 10 million rows is ~24 steps.
exercises.note: Everything in an index also exists in the table, so an index is derived data — drop one and you lose no rows, only speed. Unless it's a `UNIQUE` index, which is also enforcing a rule you'd be dropping with it.

exercises.prompt: A 1,000-page book. You want every page mentioning 'sharding.' You could read all 1,000 pages — or flip to the index at the back. What does that index give you?
choices: A sorted list of terms, each with page numbers — so you jump straight there
A faster way to read every page
Nothing you couldn't get by reading
exercises.why: That's literally what a database index is: a sorted structure mapping values to locations, so you go straight to what you want instead of reading everything. Notice three properties of that book index, because all three matter — it's SEPARATE from the content, it's SORTED (the content isn't), and it's SMALLER than the book. Those are exactly the properties that make a database index work.

exercises.prompt: So what IS a database index?
choices: A faster copy of the whole table
A separate, sorted data structure mapping column values to row locations
A cache of recent query results
A compressed version of the table
exercises.why: It's a separate structure holding one (or a few) columns, kept sorted, with pointers to where the full rows live — maintained automatically by the database. Redundant and derived should ring a bell from unit 5: an index is rebuildable state containing nothing that isn't already in the table, which is precisely why you can `DROP` an index and rebuild it without losing a single byte of data.

exercises.prompt: Finding a value among 1 million unsorted rows takes up to 1 million checks. Using a sorted index structure, roughly how many steps?
exercises.why: Each step halves the remaining search space, so it's log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 steps — twenty, versus a million. And it gets better as you grow, which is the genuinely magical part: a BILLION rows is only ~30 steps, so doubling your data adds exactly ONE step. That's why indexed lookups stay fast forever while scans fall off a cliff — they scale completely differently.

exercises.prompt: Roughly how many steps does an index need to find one row among 1 billion? (It's log₂ of a billion.)
exercises.why: 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 billion, so about 30 steps — a billion rows, thirty comparisons. Sit with the gap: 30 versus 1,000,000,000. This isn't an optimization, it's a different category of thing, and almost every 'the database got slow' story is really 'we started scanning where we used to jump'.

exercises.prompt: Without a useful index, the database performs a full table ______; with one, it jumps straight to the rows.
exercises.why: Full table scan = read every row and check it. That's the default when no index can serve your query.

exercises.prompt: An index is derived data — everything in it also exists in the table. What follows from that?
choices: You can drop and rebuild an index without losing any data
Dropping an index deletes the underlying rows
The index is the source of truth
Indexes must be backed up separately or data is lost
exercises.why: No data lives only in an index, so you can drop one and rebuild it without losing a byte. One caveat to carry, though: a `UNIQUE` index isn't pure optimization, because it also enforces a rule — drop it and you lose no data but you do lose the guarantee, which is how a duplicate-signup race gets back in. Postgres will simply refuse if a constraint depends on it. Operationally that's liberating — you can tune performance by adding and removing indexes without risking data — and it's also exactly why teams add too many of them. They feel free. The next lesson is about the bill.

exercises.title: The B-tree's shape was dictated by the disk, not by your data
exercises.body: A disk hands you a whole page — say 8KB — however little of it you wanted. A binary tree would spend one page read per comparison, narrowing the search only by half each time. A B-tree makes each node a page holding hundreds of keys, so one read narrows it hundreds of times. A billion rows end up only ~3–4 levels deep.
exercises.note: In RAM, a binary tree is perfectly good. The B-tree exists because disks deal in blocks rather than bytes — a structure whose whole design is a response to hardware it never mentions.

exercises.prompt: Databases use B-trees for indexes rather than simple binary trees. Why?
choices: A B-tree node holds hundreds of keys, matching how disks read in big blocks — so one disk read gets you hundreds of keys instead of one
exercises.why: Disks read in pages (say 8KB), so a binary tree would cost one disk read per comparison — brutal. A B-tree is wide and shallow: each node is a page holding hundreds of keys, so even a billion rows is only ~3–4 disk reads deep. This is a gorgeous example of a data structure shaped by hardware: in RAM a binary tree is perfectly fine, but on disk — where a read costs ~100µs (unit 4's ladder) — you must minimize READS rather than comparisons. The B-tree exists because disks read blocks, not bytes.

exercises.prompt: You create an index on the `email` column. What does the index actually store?
choices: A complete copy of every row
The email values, kept sorted, each with a pointer to where the full row lives
Only a list of emails, with no way back to the row
A hash of the entire row
exercises.why: Sorted values plus pointers — that's why it's small (one column, not the whole row) and why it can find you the row once it locates the value. That pointer matters more than it looks: finding the value in the index is fast, but then fetching the actual row is a separate, random read. Hold that thought, because it explains the planner's behaviour in the next lesson.

exercises.prompt: Why can an index on `created_at` efficiently answer 'all rows from last week'?
choices: It can't — indexes only do exact matches
Because the index is SORTED: once you find the start of the range, the rest sit right next to each other
exercises.why: Sortedness is what gives you ranges: find the start, then read sequentially, and you never search again. This is why sorted beats hashed for most database work — a hash index is O(1) for `= value` but completely useless for `> value` or `ORDER BY`, because hashing deliberately destroys order. B-trees give you equality AND ranges AND sorting from one structure, which is why they're the default everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Match each approach to what it gives you.

pairs.right: Read every row and check it

exercises.why: Different structures make different promises, and the B-tree's sortedness is what makes it the versatile default. Hash indexes aren't useless — for pure key-value equality lookups they're faster and smaller — they're just too narrow to be a default, because real queries want ranges and ordering sooner or later.

exercises.prompt: Your query ends with `ORDER BY created_at`, and there's an index on `created_at`. What's the bonus?
choices: The index is already in sorted order, so the database can skip the sort step entirely
The rows come back in random order
exercises.why: An index doesn't just find rows — it can hand them over already in order, eliminating an expensive sort. Sorting a large result set can dominate a query's cost, and if it doesn't fit in memory it spills to disk and collapses; a surprising share of 'nothing changed, but it got slow' incidents are a query that quietly started sorting on disk as the data grew.

exercises.prompt: What's the essential property that makes an index fast?
choices: It's sorted, so the database can eliminate most of the data with each step instead of checking rows one by one
exercises.why: Order is the whole trick: sortedness lets you discard half — or in a B-tree, the vast majority — of the remaining candidates at every step. Which is also the clue to every index's limitation: an index can only help when your query aligns with the order it's stored in, so ask it a question that doesn't match its ordering and it may as well not exist. That's the theme of lesson 4.

exercises.title: Every index you add is another structure the database must write on every change
exercises.body: An index is a copy, and a copy has to be kept true. `INSERT` one row into a table carrying three indexes and the database does four writes: the row, plus an entry in each index — every one of them landing in a sorted structure that may have to split a page to make room. The reads got faster. The writes paid for them.
exercises.note: So a write's cost scales with how many indexes sit on the table — and nobody notices, because the query you sped up is the one you were watching.

exercises.prompt: You add 5 indexes to a table to make reads fast. What happens to writes?
choices: Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` must now update all 5 indexes too, so writes get slower
exercises.why: An index is a copy that must be kept in sync, so every write to the table pays to maintain every index on it. This is the central tradeoff of the unit: indexes buy read speed with write speed and disk, and a table with 15 indexes can be several times slower to write than the same table with two. There is no free lookup — you're moving the cost, not removing it.

exercises.prompt: What does each additional index cost you? Select all.
choices: More memory — indexes compete for cache
Slower reads on the indexed column
exercises.why: Writes, disk, and memory pressure — reads on that column get FASTER, which is the entire point of paying the other three. The memory one is quietly important: your indexes compete with your data for the database's cache, so enough unnecessary indexes and you evict the hot data you actually needed. A pile of 'harmless' indexes can slow down reads they have nothing to do with.

exercises.prompt: A team adds an index on every column, 'just in case.' Result?
choices: Writes crawl, disk balloons, the planner has more ways to choose wrong — and most of those indexes are never used at all
exercises.why: Unused indexes are pure cost: maintained on every single write, read by nobody — 'just in case' is a bill you pay forever for a benefit you never collect. Real databases track index usage statistics, so finding and dropping dead indexes is a classic, high-value, low-risk cleanup. It's common to find tables where half the indexes have never been used since the day they were created.

exercises.prompt: You have an index on `country`. For `WHERE country = 'US'`, where 90% of rows are US, the planner does a full scan anyway. Why?
choices: It's a bug in the planner
Reading 90% of the table via an index means randomly jumping to nearly every row — streaming the whole table sequentially is genuinely faster
Indexes don't work on text columns
exercises.why: The index gives you a pointer, then you pay a random read to fetch each row — doing that for 90% of the table is far slower than just reading the table straight through. It's sequential-vs-random again, the same physics behind unit 6's write-ahead log, and the planner is right while your intuition is wrong. It also reveals the rule governing lesson 4: an index only helps when it's SELECTIVE — when it narrows to a small fraction of the table.

exercises.prompt: Which is cheaper to use as an indexed primary key: an auto-incrementing id, or a random UUID?
choices: The auto-incrementing id — new values always append at the end of the index, while random UUIDs scatter writes across the whole structure
The random UUID — randomness spreads load evenly
exercises.why: Sequential ids append to one hot spot at the end of the index; random UUIDs land anywhere, forcing the B-tree to split pages all over and destroying cache locality. This is a famous, real performance problem — random UUID primary keys can dramatically slow inserts on large tables — and it's exactly why UUIDv7 (time-ordered) was standardized: you keep global uniqueness but restore write locality. A great example of a 'neutral' id choice quietly being a storage decision.

exercises.prompt: A write-heavy audit log: billions of appends, queried only during rare investigations. Slide toward how many indexes you'd add.
exercises.why: Write-heavy and read-rarely means indexes are almost pure cost — you'd pay on every one of billions of writes to speed up a query someone runs twice a year. Same rule as the social feed, pointed the other way: put the work where the traffic isn't. Here the traffic is writes, so keep the write path lean and accept that the rare investigation takes a slow scan. That's the correct trade, not a compromise.

exercises.title: An index earns its keep by narrowing, and matching 95% of the table narrows nothing
exercises.body: *Selectivity* is the fraction of rows a lookup eliminates. `WHERE email = 'x@y.com'` leaves one row out of ten million: superb. `WHERE is_active = true`, where 95% of rows are true, leaves 95% — and reaching 95% of a table through an index is *slower* than scanning it, because you'd jump around the disk to fetch nearly every row anyway.
exercises.note: Selectivity belongs to the query, not the column. That same `is_active` index is excellent for `WHERE is_active = false` — 5% of rows, highly selective. One column, two opposite verdicts.

exercises.prompt: You index a boolean `is_active` column where 95% of rows are true. Does it help `WHERE is_active = true`?
choices: Barely — it matches 95% of rows, so it isn't selective, and the planner will likely scan anyway
exercises.why: An index earns its keep by NARROWING, and matching 95% of the table narrows nothing — so you pay the write cost for essentially no read benefit. Rule of thumb: index high-cardinality columns (many distinct values — `email`, `user_id`), because indexing a boolean is usually cargo cult. But note the subtlety: the SAME column can be worth indexing for the opposite query, since `WHERE is_active = false` matches only 5% of rows and is highly selective. Selectivity is a property of the QUERY, not just the column — and if that rare case is all you ever query, a partial index (one defined with its own `WHERE` clause so it physically contains only those 5% of rows) is smaller still.

exercises.prompt: You have a composite index on `(last_name, first_name)`. Which query can use it?
exercises.why: A composite index sorts by the first column, then the second — exactly like a phone book sorted by last name, then first. You can find all the Lovelaces instantly; you cannot find all the Adas, because they're scattered across every last name. This is the leftmost prefix rule, one of the most misunderstood things in databases: an index on `(a, b, c)` serves queries on `a`, on `(a, b)`, and on `(a, b, c)` — but NOT on `b` alone, `c` alone, or `(b, c)`. Column ORDER is a real design decision, not a formality.

exercises.prompt: Given an index on `(a, b, c)`, which queries can use it? Select all.
exercises.why: Leftmost prefix: you must start at `a`. Anything beginning with `a` can use the index; `b` on its own can't, because the index isn't sorted by `b` — it's sorted by `b` only within each `a`. The practical consequence: one well-ordered composite index on `(a, b, c)` can replace separate indexes on `a` and on `(a, b)` — three queries served, one index maintained, which is how you get fast reads without drowning your writes.

exercises.prompt: Query: `SELECT email FROM users WHERE email = 'x@y.com'`, with an index on `email`. Why might the database answer this without reading the table at all?
choices: Because the index already contains every column the query asks for
It can't — it always has to read the row
exercises.why: The index holds email values, and an email is all the query wants — so when every column a query needs is already in the index, the database can answer from the index alone and skip fetching the row. That's a covering index (an index-only scan), and it's a bigger deal than it sounds: you skip the random read to fetch the row, which is often the expensive half. It's why engineers sometimes add a column to an index purely so it can answer a whole query alone, without ever filtering on that column. One caveat worth carrying: Postgres still consults its visibility map and will fetch the row anyway if the page isn't marked all-visible, so 'index-only' is a best case rather than a promise.

exercises.prompt: How do you find out whether your query is actually using an index?
choices: Run `EXPLAIN` — the database shows you the plan it chose
exercises.why: Don't guess — ask. `EXPLAIN` shows the plan: whether you got a sequential scan or an index lookup, and what it estimates the cost to be. This is arguably the highest-leverage database skill for an average engineer, because a huge share of 'the database is slow' turns out to be one missing index and `EXPLAIN` finds it in about ten seconds. Learning to read a query plan pays for itself in a week.

exercises.prompt: A query filters `WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'open'`, then sorts `ORDER BY created_at`. Which single composite index best serves it?
exercises.why: Equality columns first (`user_id`, `status`) to narrow hard, then the sort column (`created_at`) — the index jumps to user 42's open rows, and they're already in `created_at` order, so the sort step disappears too. The general recipe: equality columns first, then your range/sort column. Get it backwards — `(created_at, user_id, status)` — and it's nearly useless here, because you'd have to scan every date to find user 42. Same columns, opposite outcome.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest one-sentence summary of indexing?
choices: Index every column so every query is fast
An index is a derived, sorted copy that trades write speed and disk for read speed — so index deliberately: for real queries, on selective columns, in the right order, and verify with `EXPLAIN`
Avoid indexes; they slow down writes
Let the database figure it out automatically
exercises.why: Both extremes are wrong: indexes are a deliberate purchase, spending write throughput and disk to buy read latency, and it's only a good deal when the index actually serves a query you really run. Step back and notice this is unit 5's lesson wearing new clothes — an index is a derived copy that buys speed and costs consistency work. The only difference is the database does the syncing for you, and bills you on every write.
